newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Howe, Hawke upbeat over future of Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Howe, Hawke upbeat over future of Hong Kong.

text.p: Two key political figures at the time of the 1984 Sino-British treaty on Hong Kong's handover were upbeat on the future of the British colony after it returns to Chinese rule later this year.

Britain's Lord Howe, foreign secretary in then-Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher's government when the treaty was signed, said he believed China's communist leaders were serious about making the treaty work.

"They should be given sympathy and support," Howe said, adding that leaders in Beijing were intent on making a success of the "one country, two systems" policy that will allow capitalist Hong Kong to co-exist with the communist mainland.
Bob Hawke, Australian prime minister at the time, told the same luncheon he was optimistic about Hong Kong's future.

"I certainly have absolutely no doubt about Hong Kong's capacity -- the capacity of its business leaders and its workers to continue into the future to adapt to economic challenges as they have done in the past," he said.
Free-wheeling and wealthy Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.

Although Beijing has promised the territory a large degree of autonomy and the business community has generally discounted the likelihood of disruptions, worries persist about human rights, freedom of the press and other social issues.
Hawke said Hong Kong was increasingly tied into China.

"Despite the political controversy between the Hong Kong administration and China, which has marked the latter years of the transition period, this dramatic growth in Hong Kong has been characterised by the increasing integration with the mainland," Hawke said.
